title: Subtree at a Search Key
statement:
You get the root of a binary search tree with distinct values: everything in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node, everything in its right subtree is larger. You also get a number target.

Find the node whose value is target and return the subtree that hangs from it (the node together with all its descendants). If no node has that value, return an empty tree.

Trees are written in level order with null for missing children; an empty tree is [].

examples.why: 3 is smaller than 8, so it is on the left. It comes back with both of its children.
10 would have to be in the left subtree of 12, and that spot is empty. There is no need to look anywhere else.
A leaf is a subtree of size one.

hints: At any node you compare target with the node's value. What does each of the three outcomes tell you?
If target is smaller, it can only be in the left subtree. The whole right side can be ignored.
Walk down from the root, going left or right after each comparison. Stop at a match or when you fall off the tree.

explain.intuition:
The search-tree rule turns every node into a signpost. If target is smaller than the node, it cannot be anywhere on the right, so you step left; if it is larger, you step right. Each step throws away a whole subtree, which is exactly binary search, just on a tree.

The node you stop on is the subtree: returning the node returns everything below it. If you fall off the tree, the value is not there.
steps: While node exists and its value is not target, move to node.left if target is smaller, otherwise to node.right.
Return node. It is either the match or null (an empty tree).
pitfalls: Searching both subtrees like in a general binary tree. It still works but ignores the ordering and costs O(n) instead of O(height).
Mixing up the direction: smaller values are on the left.
Copying the subtree. The node already links to all of its descendants; just return it.

complexity.time: O(h), where h is the height of the tree

solutions.title: Search the whole tree
solutions.idea: Ignore the ordering and look in both subtrees recursively. Correct, but visits every node in the worst case.

solutions.title: Walk down using the ordering
solutions.idea: Each comparison tells you which side the target must be on, so one root-to-leaf path is enough.

followups: Return the node with the largest value that is still ≤ target instead (the floor). What changes in the walk?
The tree can be very unbalanced, like a linked list. What is the worst-case cost, and how do self-balancing trees avoid it?
